profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between a memory clinic physician lead and a primary-care-based dementia care coordinator at a large health system that is expanding its chronic disease management model to dementia. The team is aligning how newly diagnosed dementia patients will transition from the memory clinic into longitudinal support, including what gets handed off after the diagnostic visit, when patients are considered appropriate for routine follow-up versus active navigation, and how caregiver needs are incorporated into the shared workflow. The agenda is to review current progress on the dementia pathway, confirm the handoff sequence after diagnosis visits, clarify follow-up timing for patients labeled as stable, and make sure both teams can use the same shared materials without duplicating work. The expected outcome is an apparently aligned plan for who sends the care plan, which patients go to routine follow-up, and how caregiver check-ins are folded into ongoing coordination.

members.name: Dr. Elena Ruiz
members.expertise: Geriatric psychiatry, dementia diagnosis, behavioral symptom management, outpatient memory clinic workflows
members.background: Dr. Ruiz leads the diagnostic workup program for patients referred with cognitive decline and has spent the last 8 years building standardized visit templates and post-diagnosis recommendations inside the health system EHR.
members.private_state: She wants the new pathway to fit within existing physician documentation practices and avoid creating extra clinic tasks for her already overbooked specialists, while still appearing supportive of caregiver-centered care.
hidden_assumptions: When teams say 'care plan,' they mean the physician-authored post-visit plan in the EHR problem list and after-visit summary.
A patient is 'stable' if there has been no recent medication issue, delirium concern, emergency visit, or major safety event that requires specialist review.
Caregiver support is part of dementia management mainly when it directly changes the patient's clinical safety or adherence.
The memory clinic's finalized note is the canonical shared artifact, and downstream teams will adapt from it rather than maintaining a parallel document.

members.name: Jasmine Lee
members.role: RN Dementia Care Coordinator, Primary Care Network
members.expertise: Care navigation, chronic disease follow-up, caregiver coaching, community resource linkage, telephone triage
members.background: Jasmine coordinates longitudinal support for medically complex older adults across six primary care sites and has recently begun adapting chronic care management processes for patients with dementia and their family caregivers.
members.private_state: She wants memory clinic handoffs to arrive in a form her team can immediately use with families, and she is trying to protect her nurses from being blamed for missed caregiver needs later on.
hidden_assumptions: When teams say 'care plan,' they mean the family-facing action sheet that lists behavior triggers, supervision needs, local resources, and who to call for what.
A patient is 'stable' only if the caregiver can manage day-to-day needs without repeated coaching calls, crisis concerns, or new functional decline at home.
A 'caregiver check-in' automatically includes some burden/screening component and resource counseling, because dementia management is inseparable from caregiver capacity.
If the diagnostic visit is complete, the coordinator can rely on the handoff materials already reflecting the latest agreed pathway rather than checking for older clinic versions.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the care plan
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the 'care plan' will be sent after the diagnostic visit.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Ruiz means the structured physician treatment/recommendation section in the EHR note plus after-visit summary.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Jasmine means the caregiver-facing coordination document used by nurses for follow-up calls and community referrals.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In chronic care programs, 'care plan' is a familiar umbrella term that sounds standardized; both assume the other is using the local default meaning and have no reason to ask what format is meant.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as stable for routine follow-up
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that 'stable' patients can move to routine follow-up instead of active weekly navigation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Ruiz means medically and behaviorally unchanged from a specialist standpoint, with no urgent safety, medication, or diagnostic issues.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Jasmine means manageable at home with a caregiver who is coping, no repeated support calls, and no meaningful recent decline in daily functioning.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'stable' is routinely used as shorthand in clinical coordination, and both speakers believe they are discussing the same low-intensity subgroup because the mismatch lies in the threshold, not the overall direction.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the caregiver check-in
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the coordinator will do a 'caregiver check-in' after the diagnosis visit.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Ruiz assumes this means a brief operational call to confirm the family understood the diagnosis, has follow-up appointments, and knows whom to contact if behaviors worsen.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Jasmine assumes this includes burden assessment, discussion of burnout risk, review of supervision strain, and connection to respite or support resources if needed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both see caregiver contact as obviously important in dementia, the phrase feels sufficiently precise; the difference is in how much is naturally included, not whether it should happen.

turns.inner_thought: I need this pathway to feel like an extension of existing chronic disease coordination, not a brand-new workflow dumped on the memory clinic. If we can anchor everything to the diagnostic note and standard after-visit documentation, my physicians won't have to maintain extra forms. I can be supportive of caregiver-centered care as long as it doesn't create another specialist-owned task list.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The goal from my side is to keep the dementia pathway as close as possible to the way we already coordinate other chronic conditions, and I’d really like us to finalize what happens right after the diagnostic visit so there’s a clean handoff.

turns.inner_thought: What I need is a usable care plan my nurses can pick up immediately without reconstructing the visit from a long specialist note. If that comes over promptly after diagnosis day, we can start family outreach before problems snowball. I should make sure timing is explicit, because otherwise our team gets blamed later for missed caregiver needs.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Our team is ready to take people once the care plan comes over, so I just want to confirm the timing on that handoff after the diagnosis day.

turns.inner_thought: The signed note is the authoritative document. Once I sign it, the treatment recommendations and post-visit plan are in the chart and the after-visit summary is set. That should be enough for downstream teams to work from; I really don't want anyone expecting a separate clinic-generated document. Usually next business day is realistic and protects physician time.
turns.utterance: From our end, the care plan should go out once my note is signed, which is usually by the next business day. That way primary care coordination can start from the finalized visit.

turns.inner_thought: Great—if the care plan lands by next business day, my nurses can use it to guide those first outreach calls with families and organize the follow-up work. I’m assuming it will already reflect the practical pieces we need for home support and who is doing what, so we won’t have to chase older versions or fill in gaps ourselves.
turns.utterance: That timing works. If we have the care plan by then, my nurses can use it to structure the family calls and the next steps on our side.

turns.inner_thought: I need stable patients off intensive specialist touchpoints quickly. If there's no urgent medication issue, no delirium concern, no emergency visit, and no major safety event needing our review, they do not need ongoing active navigation from the memory clinic. We have to preserve capacity for complex consults.
turns.utterance: One thing I’d like to lock in is that patients who are stable after diagnosis move fairly quickly into routine follow-up, so the memory clinic can stay focused on the more acute consults.

turns.inner_thought: I agree in principle. If things are manageable at home and the caregiver is coping without repeated calls or new decline, they shouldn’t sit in active weekly navigation. We need to save the closer-touch support for the families who are really struggling day to day.
turns.utterance: I agree. Stable patients probably shouldn’t stay in intensive navigation, and we can reserve the closer contact for families who are having a harder time at home.

turns.inner_thought: Even if they're otherwise stable, I do want one follow-up touch after the diagnosis so families don't feel abandoned. For me that means a brief operational call: confirm they understood the diagnosis discussion, got the appointments, and know what to do if symptoms worsen. It should be lightweight and not turn into a major new assessment process.
turns.utterance: I would still want a caregiver check-in within about two weeks, just so families don’t feel dropped right after the diagnosis conversation.

turns.inner_thought: Two weeks is reasonable. In our world, a caregiver check-in absolutely includes burden screening, assessing strain, and offering respite or community resources if needed. That’s standard dementia support, and it protects my nurses from being told later that we never asked. I’ll frame it as part of normal outreach.
turns.utterance: Yes, a two-week caregiver check-in is very doable. We can fold that into our outreach so there’s an early touchpoint after the visit.

turns.inner_thought: After that initial call, if there are still no urgent behavior, medication, or safety issues, I’d expect routine specialist follow-up around six months. I don't want routine cases getting bounced back to us sooner just because families need general coaching; the clinic should re-engage when something clinically escalates.
turns.utterance: And if the patient remains stable after that, I’d expect routine specialist follow-up at roughly six months unless something escalates sooner.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, so we’ll watch for the care plan after signed visits, complete the caregiver check-in, and only send people back sooner if they’re not stable from a home-management standpoint. I’m comfortable with that as long as our team can act from the handoff materials and intensify support when caregivers are struggling.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. We’ll watch for the care plan after signed visits, do the caregiver check-in, and route only the unstable cases back sooner.
